Chest drain care and removal. Monitoring, care and removal, step by step.

Step one. Know where the drain sits and why. Know each part of the system: the collection chamber, the water seal, which acts as a one-way valve, and the suction control. Know expected and abnormal output, and when gravity or suction drainage is used.
Step two. Spot complications early: infection, dislodgement, kinking, and surgical emphysema. Assess breath sounds, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation.
Step three. Check the system. Keep the unit upright and below the chest, with no kinks or loops. Check the output volume and colour, any air leak, and that suction is set as ordered.
Step four. Before removal, check the order, and confirm the X-ray and clinical criteria are met. Identify the patient and obtain verbal consent.

Step five. Give analgesia as prescribed. Assemble the items and check expiry dates. Perform hand hygiene, put on gloves, position the patient with an Inco-pad under the drain, put on protective equipment, and open the sterile dressing pack.
Step six. Critical point. If the patient has more than one drain, and one or more will stay in, clamp those before removing the specified drain.

Step seven. Critical point. Remove the old dressing, use hand rub, and put on sterile gloves. Clean the site with aseptic technique, as per the wound dressing policy, and make sure the stoma will be sealed once the drain is out.

Step eight. Critical point. Cut the sutures safely and free the tube. Teach the breathing cycle first. Remove the drain during a positive pressure breath, or on expiration, on the third breath. Then ask the patient to breathe normally.
Step nine. Apply a petroleum-based dressing, followed by several layers of gauze. Assess breathing and vital signs, and arrange a chest X-ray, or echo where applicable.
Step ten. Reassure and educate the patient and family, minimise discomfort, follow infection prevention and any isolation precautions, and report abnormalities promptly.

Step eleven. Document the site, the drainage amount, colour and consistency, the system and suction settings, breathing and vital signs before and after any intervention, tubing checks, and the removal, including how the patient tolerated it.
Watch, take the quiz, then get signed off.
